lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Isn't that Heracles? It can't be anyone else — by Heracles. The bow, the club, the lion-skin, the sheer size — it's him all over. And yet he's dead? Son of Zeus and he's dead? Tell me, O Glorious Victor — are you a corpse? I used to sacrifice to you up on the surface. As a god.
lines.note: Diogenes delivers this with the tone of a man noting a minor scheduling irregularity.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: And you were right to sacrifice. Heracles himself is up in heaven with the gods, and he has Hebe — lovely-ankled Hebe — as his wife. I am merely his image.
lines.note: Heracles says this with enormous dignity. He has prepared this speech.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What do you mean, 'image of a god'? Is it actually possible to be half a god — and dead the other half?
lines.note: Genuine curiosity. Not sarcasm. Yet.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Yes. He didn't die. I did — his likeness.
lines.note: Doubling down.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I see. So he sent you down as a substitute — a man in his place — to pay his debt to Pluto. You're dead on his behalf.
lines.note: Still perfectly calm.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Something like that.
lines.note: Said too quickly.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But Aeacus is thorough. He's famously thorough. How did he fail to spot that you weren't the real one — and let in a counterfeit Heracles?
lines.note: The tone of a man raising a legitimate procedural concern.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Because I was an exact resemblance.
lines.note: Beginning to sense this is not going well.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Right. An exact resemblance — as in, indistinguishable. So consider the possibility that you've got it backwards: that you're the real Heracles, and what married Hebe up among the gods is the image.
lines.note: Diogenes presents this as a helpful alternative hypothesis.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You are impertinent and you talk too much. Keep mocking me and you'll find out very shortly what kind of god's image I am. [pause]
lines.note: The threat is genuine. It only makes things worse, and he knows it the moment he says it.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: The bow is out and ready — I can see that. But what exactly am I supposed to be afraid of? I'm already dead. [pause] But tell me — by your Heracles up there — back when he was alive, were you with him then too? Floating alongside as his image? Or were you one being during life, and when you died, you split — he flew off to the gods and you, the image, came here, as was only fitting?
lines.note: Entirely genial. This is genuine philosophical inquiry to Diogenes.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: I really shouldn't dignify this with a response. But — fine — listen. Whatever part of Heracles came from Amphitryon: that part died. That part is me — all of it. Whatever part came from Zeus is up in heaven with the gods.
lines.note: Heracles has moved from dignity to the defensive. He is explaining himself to Diogenes, which is already a loss.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Now I understand perfectly. You're saying Alcmene gave birth to two Heracles at the same time — one from Amphitryon, one from Zeus. So you were secret twins all along, with the same mother.
lines.note: Said as a helpful summary, completely straight-faced.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: No, you idiot — we were both the same person.
lines.note: With feeling.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: It's not easy to follow — two Heracles rolled into one composite. Unless you were some kind of centaur situation: man and god fused together into a single creature.
lines.note: Still perfectly reasonable.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Doesn't everyone, in your view, consist of two things — soul and body? So what's the obstacle to the soul — which came from Zeus — being in heaven, while the mortal part, meaning me, is here among the dead?
lines.note: Heracles has found a philosophical foothold and is pleased with himself for a moment.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: That would be a perfectly good argument, my dear Son-of-Amphitryon, if you were a body. But you're a bodiless image. So you're now in danger of making Heracles into three things.
lines.note: Gently.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Three? How three?
lines.note: He shouldn't have asked.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Like this: one version is up in heaven; you — the image — are here with us; and the body has dissolved and is already dust. That's three. And you'll want to start thinking about which of the three gets a third father.
lines.note: Diogenes ticks these off with mild academic interest, as though annotating a diagram.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You're insolent and you're a sophist. Who are you, anyway?
lines.note: Retreating to the classic question of last resort.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: The image of Diogenes of Sinope. As for the real me — not, I assure you, up among the immortal gods — [chuckles] but here, keeping company with the finest of the dead, and laughing at Homer and all that magnificent nonsense.
lines.note: The Homeric echo ('among the immortal gods') is deliberate self-deprecation-as-punchline. Diogenes is enjoying himself.
